title: Deconstructing The Philidor Defence  | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We open e4, Black replies e5, and we head for our Four Knights Scotch.
Black develops to c6. A bonus of this system: you needn't learn a separate line against the Petrov — the knight to c3 covers it, saving work.
Black plays d6 — a souped-up Philidor, quite passive; it doesn't change our plan.
We play d4 as usual — with Black so passive, why not.
The knights come off and our queen recaptures on d4 — Black often trades everything here, but our queen sits beautifully.

Black develops the knight to f6. Note: a later ...c5 is no threat — it would only weaken d6 badly and hand us the d5-square as an outpost for a knight. Don't fear your queen being attacked; it isn't inherently dangerous.
We develop the bishop to g5, natural and strong — and since our queen has already left d1, castling long is on the cards.
Black plays the bishop to e7. The principled path is to castle queenside and then steamroll on the kingside and in the centre.
Black plays ...c5, in love with hitting the queen. But don't rush to move it — the best move here isn't a queen move at all: it's the bishop check on b5.

We check with the bishop on b5. Black will block with ...Bd7 and we trade the light-squared bishops — excellent positionally: d5 grows even weaker, and with the light bishops gone nothing guards it, so we can take the f6-knight whenever we like and plant a knight on d5.

Black blocks with the bishop to d7. Careful, though — recapturing at once allows the famous ...Nxd7 trap, and then grabbing g7 would run into ...Bxg5 with check. Played accurately the resulting endgame is still much better for White — Black's d6-pawn is doomed — but it's an important line to calculate.
We take on d7 with check.

Black recaptures with the queen on d7. Now a good square for our queen: e3 walks into ...Ng4, and d3 blocks our rook — we want the d1-rook to x-ray down the file, so we clear it. That leaves c4: active and pressing, with ...b5 harmless since we guard it twice. And the x-ray is the point — it enables e5.

We play the queen to c4. Now e5 is almost a no-brainer — it forces the f6-knight back and Black's position teeters, all because ...c5 wrecked the centre. The x-ray on the d-pawn is exactly why e5 works: meet ...d5 with a capture on f6, and if Black takes our queen we take his and emerge a piece up. From here we simply release the tension and collect — the weakened c5-pawn falls, and with a pin — while our rook heads to e1 and a knight to d5, tremendous energy in our pieces.
